title: Backrest of a Litter
medium: Mixed media: wood, gold alloy, pigment, shell inlay

image.credit: Cleveland Museum of Art, John L. Severance Fund (1952.233)
image.license: Public domain. Released under the Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access program

altText: A flat, wide panel made of wood and decorated with metal, pigment and shell. Small figures are arranged across its surface, and there are holes along the bottom edge.

source.verifiedBy: Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access API record (title, creators, creation_date, technique, culture, creditline, description, did_you_know, images.web.url, share_license_status CC0)

context: A mixed-media object made by the Chimú people of the North Coast of the Central Andes. The Cleveland Museum of Art dates it by radiocarbon to 1185–1275. It was the back support of a litter, a seat that porters carried.

descriptions.k: Look at the flat panel with little figures on it. It is made of wood, shiny metal and shell. Can you find the figures? Which one do you see first? Point to the holes at the bottom.
descriptions.g12: This panel was the back of a seat called a litter. People carried a litter on poles, like a very special chair. It was made of wood, metal, paint and shell by the Chimú people long ago. Find the figures on the panel. What do you think they are doing?
descriptions.g35: The Chimú people of the Andes made this backrest for a litter, a seat that porters carried. The panel combines wood, gold alloy, pigment and shell. Its figures probably show a Chimú lord and four officials. Look closely at how the figures are arranged. Why might a leader's seat be decorated this way?
descriptions.g68: This backrest belonged to a litter, a seat carried by porters, made by the Chimú of the North Coast of the Central Andes. The museum dates it by radiocarbon to 1185–1275. The figures likely represent a lord and four officials, and the holes at the bottom probably held a beam under the seat. How might the figures show rank and power? Use details to explain.
descriptions.g910: This Chimú litter backrest (1185–1275, by radiocarbon) joins wood, gold alloy, pigment and shell inlay. The figures likely represent a lord with four officials, and the holes at the base probably held the beam that supported the seat. Cinnabar, a toxic mercury compound, colored the red areas. How do the materials and arrangement communicate status, and what questions remain about the figures' meaning?
descriptions.g1112: Made by the Chimú in the late Intermediate period, this backrest turns a functional part of a litter into a display of authority. Wood, gold alloy, shell inlay and cinnabar-based pigment were combined, and the figures likely show a lord and four officials. How does the object bind craft, costly materials and social hierarchy, and what limits does a radiocarbon date range place on our reading of it?

k.daily: Find the little figures on the panel. How many can you count?
k.emotion: This panel is for a special seat. How does it look to you: fancy or plain?
k.observation: Point to a place where you see shiny metal or shell. What do you notice?
k.analysis: Look at the holes at the bottom. Where are they on the panel?
k.line: Trace the edge of the panel with your finger. Where does it go?
k.shape: Find a figure. What shapes do you see in its body?
k.color: Find the biggest patch of color. What color is it?
k.texture: Imagine touching the wood, the metal and the shell. Which would feel smoothest?
k.space: Show with your hands how wide the panel is. Which looks longer, side to side or top to bottom?
k.light: Which part of the panel looks shiniest, like it catches light?
k.meaning: Someone sat in front of this panel. Who do you think it was?
k.culture: People carried this seat on poles. Who might have carried it?
k.technique: The artists used wood, metal and shell. Which one do you see most?
k.personal: If you had a special seat, what would you put on its back?
k.critical: What would you like to ask the people who made this?

g12.daily: Why do you think the makers put so many small figures on one panel?
g12.emotion: What feeling do you get from a seat decorated with figures, metal and shell?
g12.observation: Look at the panel for one minute. Tell a partner five things you found.
g12.analysis: Which figure do you look at first, and what makes your eyes go there?
g12.line: How do the lines of the figures and the edges of the panel guide your eyes?
g12.shape: What shapes do you find in the figures, and which ones repeat?
g12.color: How does the red background make the figures stand out?
g12.texture: How would the wood and the shell feel different if you could touch them?
g12.space: How can you tell that the panel is wide and flat, like the back of a seat?
g12.light: Where might shell or metal sparkle when the sun shines on this panel?
g12.meaning: The figures probably show a lord and four officials. What clues might tell them apart?
g12.culture: This panel was part of a seat carried by porters. What does that tell you about the person who sat there?
g12.technique: How did the artists use wood, gold alloy and shell to make a picture?
g12.personal: If you made a special chair for a leader, what would you put on the back?
g12.critical: Why might the museum say 'probably' when talking about the holes at the bottom?

g35.daily: Which details on the panel make you think this belonged to someone important?
g35.emotion: What mood does the red background and the row of figures give this object?
g35.observation: Describe one figure on the panel. What does it wear or hold, and how is it placed?
g35.analysis: How are the figures arranged to show that some matter more than others?
g35.line: How do the repeated lines and borders organize the surface of the panel?
g35.shape: What shapes make up the figures, and how are they repeated across the panel?
g35.color: The museum notes that cinnabar colored the red background and faces. How does a strong red affect how you see the figures?
g35.texture: How do wood, metal and shell make different surfaces on one object?
g35.space: The holes at the bottom held a beam under the seat. How does that help you picture how the panel was used?
g35.light: How might light have made the shell and gold alloy look different from the painted areas?
g35.meaning: What might the four officials near the lord be doing for him, and how can the panel show it?
g35.culture: What does this litter backrest tell us about how the Chimú showed rank?
g35.technique: Why would an artist combine wood, gold alloy, pigment and shell on one panel?
g35.personal: What would it feel like to be carried on a litter like this, and what would others think when they saw you?
g35.critical: Why do you think the museum says the figures likely show a lord and officials instead of saying so for sure?

g68.daily: How might the placement of the figures communicate rank among the lord and his officials?
g68.emotion: How does the combination of red pigment and shiny materials shape the mood of the panel?
g68.observation: Compare the way the figures are made with the way the borders are made. What differences do you see?
g68.analysis: How does the layout use repetition and symmetry to organize the whole backrest?
g68.line: How do the lines in the figures and the frame lead your eye across the surface?
g68.shape: How do the shapes of the figures relate to the rectangular form of the panel?
g68.color: The red areas were colored with cinnabar, which is toxic. What might the Chimú have gained by using such a costly pigment?
g68.texture: How do the different materials create contrast of surface, and which seems most precious?
g68.space: How could the holes at the base and the panel's width help you imagine the full litter?
g68.light: How might shell inlay and gold alloy have reacted to firelight or sunlight compared with the pigment?
g68.meaning: If the figures are a lord and four officials, what story about authority might they tell?
g68.culture: How could a litter and its backrest show the Chimú ideas of power, wealth and service?
g68.technique: What skills did makers need to join wood, metal, shell and pigment on one object?
g68.personal: What objects today show a person's status the way this litter did, and how are they similar or different?
g68.critical: The museum dates this to 1185–1275 by radiocarbon with 95.4% probability. How does a date range change what we can say about it?

g910.daily: How does the arrangement of the figures set up a hierarchy that viewers could read at a glance?
g910.emotion: What tone do the costly materials and the strong red establish for anyone who saw the litter carried past?
g910.observation: Examine how the figures and their borders are rendered. What do they reveal about the makers' priorities?
g910.analysis: How does the panel use repetition and balance to structure a crowd of figures?
g910.line: How do the contours of the figures and the frame work together to organize the surface?
g910.shape: How do the figures' forms respond to the wide, flat shape of the panel?
g910.color: How does the use of cinnabar, a toxic mercury compound, show the value placed on a strong red in this context?
g910.texture: How does the contrast between wood, metal and shell create emphasis on certain figures or areas?
g910.space: How do the panel's size and the holes at the base help you reconstruct how it fit into the litter?
g910.light: How would changing light conditions have altered the way the inlay and metal read against the pigment?
g910.meaning: If the figures likely depict a lord with four officials, what does that choice reveal about how rulers wanted to be seen?
g910.culture: How does a portable seat differ from a fixed throne in how it displays a ruler's power to a public?
g910.technique: How does the combination of materials reflect the resources and workshops available to Chimú rulers?
g910.personal: What does this object make you consider about how people use objects to carry their own authority from place to place?
g910.critical: What alternative readings of the figures are possible, and what evidence would you need to test them?

g1112.daily: How does the panel use hierarchical arrangement to make social order visible, and what features of the figures support that reading?
g1112.emotion: In what ways might the saturated red and reflective materials have shaped how others felt in the presence of the person carried?
g1112.observation: Scan the junctions between figures, borders and inlay. What do they reveal about how the makers planned the whole surface?
g1112.analysis: How does the compositional logic of the backrest balance a central authority against attendant figures?
g1112.line: How do the linear structures of the figures and frame make the surface readable at the distance of a procession?
g1112.shape: How do the figural forms negotiate the wide rectangle of the panel, and what might that say about design priorities?
g1112.color: What does the use of toxic cinnabar suggest about the cost, risk and meaning the Chimú attached to red?
g1112.texture: How might the interplay of organic wood and precious metal and shell have expressed the wealth available to Chimú elites?
g1112.space: How do the beam holes at the base complicate any reading of the panel as a purely decorative image, and what do they imply about use?
g1112.light: How might shifting light during a procession have animated the inlay and metal, and how does that affect our reading?
g1112.meaning: The museum says the figures likely depict a lord and four officials. How would you weigh that interpretation against the limits of the evidence?
g1112.culture: How does a litter backrest function as political theater, and how does that compare with other portable displays of rank?
g1112.technique: What can the mix of wood, gold alloy, shell and pigment tell us about trade, workshops and technical knowledge?
g1112.personal: How does your own sense of status symbols shape the way you approach an object made for a ruler centuries ago?
g1112.critical: A radiocarbon range of 1185–1275 gives a margin of uncertainty. What kinds of claims does that margin allow and what kinds should we avoid?

teacherNote.context: A mixed-media object (wood, gold alloy, pigment and shell inlay) made by the Chimú people of the North Coast of the Central Andes. The Cleveland Museum of Art gives a radiocarbon date of 1185–1275 and describes it as the back support of a litter carried by porters.
directions: Ask younger students to find the figures and the holes on the panel and say what they think each part was for.
Have students design a decorated backrest for a leader in their own community, choosing materials and figures.
Ask older students to discuss how radiocarbon dating gives a range of dates and how a range affects what we can say about the object.
